flashcard_questions.q: When did Shelley write Ozymandias, after hearing of an archaeological find?
Which pharaoh is the Ozymandias of the poem?
Which word shows the statue’s body is missing from its legs?
Which phrase captures the ruler’s cruel arrogance in his carved face?
Which boast is carved on the pedestal of the statue?
flashcard_questions.a: ‘Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!’

flashcard_questions.q: Why has the meaning of that boast reversed for a modern reader?
flashcard_questions.a: Nothing is left to look at, so even the greatest power crumbles.

flashcard_questions.q: Which oxymoron does Shelley use for the ruined statue?
Which sound device in ‘lone and level sands stretch’ imitates the wind?
Which short sentence creates the poem’s most dramatic caesura?
What is a caesura in poetry?
flashcard_questions.a: A pause near the middle of a line, often created by punctuation.

flashcard_questions.q: Which fourteen-line form does Shelley use for Ozymandias?
Why is Shelley’s choice of that form surprising?
flashcard_questions.a: It is traditionally used for love poetry, not for the decay of power.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the irregular rhyme scheme mirror in the poem?
Which line of the poem has eleven syllables instead of ten?
flashcard_questions.a: ‘My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings.’

flashcard_questions.q: Who tells the speaker about the ruined statue?
flashcard_questions.a: A traveller from an antique land.

notes: 15 cards: 6 quotation-recall fronts, 3 quotation-to-technique (sibilance, the oxymoron, the caesura sentence), 4 structure-and-form cards (the sonnet, why it is subverted, the irregular rhyme, the eleven-syllable line), 1 context date (1817), 1 subject identification (Ramesses II). The existing poet and 1818 publication cards were not repeated; the throne-name meaning and the pharaoh’s wives and children were dropped as flavour that no mark scheme rewards. All quotations verbatim from the lesson content.
